name: Chloe Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the depot on the industrial estate outside Saltmarsh by half six, scanning my van load off the handheld. I do the hill route out to the farms, about 140 drops, because I'm the one who knows where every gate and dog is. I'm also lead driver, so I show the new starters how to load in drop order, which nobody ever explained to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own on the coast road with the radio on, and I like that farmers wave at me now. What wears me out is the app. It sets the times, it docks you if a parcel's late, and you can't argue with it. Three nights a week I also do takeaway runs to make rent, so some days I'm in the van for thirteen hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, told you so. Half the stuff they sell as clever is just a new screen telling drivers to go faster. I'd post it in the drivers' group with a laughing face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me. The app still squeezes us, my pay is still the lowest in the depot area, and I've got less than a month's rent saved. AI being a flop doesn't make my week any easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the hill route and the three takeaway nights, same as now. I'd try to get the other drivers to join the union branch in town, because that's the only thing I've seen actually lift pay. And I'd stop buying lunch at the garage and bring sandwiches, which saves maybe twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared, just worn down, like the same week on repeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pay is the lowest around. What happens if the van breaks or you're off sick for a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm borrowing from my mum, which I hate. Last winter I had flu for five days and lost almost a whole week's money, because we're paid per drop. If AI is a flop, nothing about that changes, and that's the bit that actually keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that, if not the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parcel firms that pay the subcontractor peanuts and the subcontractor that passes it down. A robot didn't set my rate of 70 pence a parcel, a person in an office did. I'd rather fight that person than worry about computers.

say: AI flopping proves most **tech hype** was just new screens telling drivers to hurry.
The real problem is **pay per drop**, and AI was never going to fix that.
think: Nothing gets easier: my **savings** cover under a month and one sick week wipes me out.
The squeeze comes from **parcel firms** setting rates, not from any computer.
do: Keep the **hill route** and three takeaway nights to cover rent.
Sign up other drivers to the **union branch** in town this year.
Bring **packed lunches** instead of garage food to save about twenty a week.
feel: **Worn down** rather than scared, as if the same hard week repeats forever.
S0.quote: A robot didn't set my rate of 70 pence a parcel, a person in an office did.
fieldNote: Her worry exists **without AI**: per-drop pay, one month of savings and no sick pay.
She blames **people in offices** rather than technology, which steers her toward the union.
Calm voice, but a **single illness** already forced her to borrow from her mum.

steps.text: Keep the hill route and three evening takeaway shifts
Bring sandwiches to work instead of buying lunch at the garage
Recruit depot drivers to the union branch in Saltmarsh

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's office people's turn to feel what drivers have felt for years. Booking and planning going to software doesn't touch me lifting a parcel over a gate. I'd probably say that a bit smugly at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the planning bit already got taken from us years ago, the app does it. What scares me is the slow robots part. If even one of those delivery vans that drive themselves shows up on the flat routes in town, the firm won't need as many of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay on the hill route as long as I can, because robots will do the easy town streets first. Push the union to get something in writing about what happens to drivers if machines come in. I won't be buying any courses or learning any AI stuff, I just won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick in my stomach, honestly. Like hearing thunder far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn any AI tools. Why not, even if they come into the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time they bring in something new, it's to watch us closer. The last update added a camera that beeps if you touch your phone. I'm not going to help build the thing that replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who does the town centre route, he's 58 and his back's gone. Flat streets, short drops, it's exactly what they'd give a robot van. I'd worry he'd be the first one let go and nobody would hire him.

say: It's the **office workers'** turn now; booking going to software doesn't lift parcels over gates.
Drivers already lost **route planning** to the app years ago.
think: The danger is **self-driving vans** arriving slowly on the flat town routes.
Fewer town routes means the firm needs **fewer drivers**, and few local jobs exist.
do: Hold on to the **hill route**, which robots will reach last.
Press the union for a **written promise** on drivers if machines arrive.
Refuse **AI courses** and new tools on principle.
feel: **Queasy**, like hearing distant thunder that is slowly getting closer.
S1.quote: I'm not going to help build the thing that replaces me.
fieldNote: She sees new tech as **surveillance first**, which explains her refusal to learn it.
She worries about her older colleague Kev on the **flat town route**, not just herself.
Her plan rests on the **hard route** staying human, which she admits is a bet.

steps.text: Ask the manager to keep her on the rural hill route
Push the union for written terms on drivers if robot vans come

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws now, before the companies decide everything. I'd share every petition going. At work I'd say it loudly so the new lads hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? The thinking AI by 2028 doesn't matter much for driving, the app already thinks for us. But robots by 2031 means I've got about four years before someone drives my route with no driver. I'll be 31 with no savings and nothing on my CV except driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to every union meeting and get the drivers to sign up together. I'd try to put twenty a week aside, even though that's hard. I'd ask my mum if I could move back in if it comes to it, so I'm not paying rent on nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened, the kind where you keep checking your bank app at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that bank app say right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 340 in the account and rent's 520 at the start of the month. So I'm always just ahead of it, never actually ahead. A month without work and I'm in my old bedroom at Mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn new tools. With four years, would you change your mind about retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, I'm not sure. I'd want something with hands and people, like a care job, but they pay even less. I really don't know what I'd train for that a robot couldn't do by then too.

say: We need **laws now**, before companies decide what happens to drivers.
I'd share every **petition** and say it loudly to the new starters.
think: Robots by **2031** gives me about four years before my route runs without a driver.
At 31 I'd have **no savings** and only driving on my CV.
do: Get drivers to join the **union** together at every meeting.
Put aside **twenty a week**, even though money is already tight.
Ask Mum about **moving back home** if the work dries up.
feel: **Frightened**, checking the bank app at night.
Lost about **retraining**, since she can't name a safe trade.
S2.quote: About 340 in the account and rent's 520 at the start of the month.
fieldNote: She separates the two dates clearly: **thinking AI** barely matters, **robots** end her route.
Her cushion is tiny: **£340** against **£520** rent.
She softens on **retraining** but cannot see a trade that robots won't also reach.

steps.text: Sign up drivers to the union at the monthly meeting
Save twenty pounds every week from the takeaway shifts
Ask her mum about moving back home if routes are cut
Share petitions for laws protecting delivery drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: protect the drivers and make the companies pay for the changeover. I'd say five years is enough time for the government to sort it if they actually want to. I'd go to the council meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years for the thinking bit and then about three more for robots is time I'd mostly waste. I know myself, I'll keep driving till the day they take the van keys. That's 2034, so I'd be 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the route, keep the takeaway nights, and keep pushing the union for a fund that pays drivers to retrain when the robots arrive. Maybe I'd do my heavy goods licence, because big lorries might go robot later than vans. That costs money I don't have, so I'd need the union or the council to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not like the fast one. More like knowing a bill is coming next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the time. What would make you not waste it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me exactly what to do and paying for it. If the union said, here's a lorry licence course, it's free, starts in March, I'd go. I just won't gamble my own rent money on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm single right now, so there's nobody to split rent with, which is half the problem. My mum would say get an office job, but those are going first in this picture. She doesn't really get it.

say: **Five years** is enough time for government to protect drivers if it wants to.
Companies should **pay for the changeover**, not the drivers.
think: I'll probably **keep driving** until they take the van keys, around 2034.
Without a clear plan, I'd **waste** most of the warning time.
do: Keep the **route** and the takeaway nights for steady money.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** for drivers.
Do a **lorry licence** if someone else helps pay for it.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing a big bill is due next year.
S3.quote: I know myself, I'll keep driving till the day they take the van keys.
fieldNote: She is honest that **warning time** alone won't move her; she needs a paid, clear path.
She lives **alone**, so there is no second income to absorb a shock.
A **lorry licence** is her only concrete idea, and only if funded.

steps.text: Keep driving the hill route and three takeaway nights
Push the union for a fund paying drivers to retrain
Take a heavy goods licence course if the union or council pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, so let's not waste it on arguing. I'd want drivers on whatever committee plans it. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means robots around 2039, when I'm 40. That's a long way off, and I honestly might not even be driving by then. It still bothers me, because 40 with no savings is no better than 31 with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now for a few years, and build a bit of savings when the union wins a pay rise. Around 2033 I'd start the lorry licence or something with care homes. I'd want to be out of vans before the robots, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it doesn't go away. It sits there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different for you between this and the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'm grabbing at anything. In this one I can actually plan, and maybe go part-time on takeaway to study. Ten years is the difference between choosing and being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change in your life now, knowing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking of this job as just for now. I've been saying for now since I was 21. I'd actually pick something and start saving toward it.

say: **Ten years** is a real chance to do this fairly.
Drivers deserve a seat on any **planning committee**.
think: Robots around **2039** feels far off, but I'd be 40 with nothing saved.
I keep calling this job **for now**, and that's been six years.
do: Keep driving and **save** a bit when pay rises come through.
Start a **lorry or care** course around 2033.
Leave vans **before robots** arrive, not after.
feel: **Calmer**, though the worry sits quietly in the background.
S4.quote: Ten years is the difference between choosing and being pushed.
fieldNote: Time changes her tone from **grabbing** to **planning**.
Her savings gap still worries her, because ten years doesn't fix **thin pay**.
She admits she has drifted since 21, which **long warning** might finally change.

steps.text: Keep driving parcels and save part of any union pay rise
Start a lorry licence or care course around 2033
Leave van driving before robot vans reach Saltmarsh

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have four years and no money. What would help is a proper fund, run with the union, that pays drivers while they retrain. And sick pay, honestly, which would help me today in any of the five.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. If the same firms that pay us 70 pence a parcel own the robot vans, the money goes to them and we get nothing. Somebody has to decide that, and it shouldn't only be them.

headlineQuote: If the same firms that pay us 70 pence a parcel own the robot vans, the money goes to them and we get nothing.
portrait: Chloe is 27, lives **alone** near Saltmarsh, and is lead driver on the hardest rural parcel route.
She earns **per drop**, does three takeaway nights, and has under a month's rent saved.
She distrusts new tech as **surveillance**, refuses AI tools, and puts her faith in the union.
Her fear grows with the **robot dates**: four years feels like a cliff, ten like a chance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 would end her route with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A union-run **retraining fund** that pays drivers while they learn.
**Sick pay** now, which would help her in every scenario.
